title: You don’t need a revenue intelligence tool to hear customers
summary: Small sales teams don’t need a revenue intelligence platform to learn why deals are lost. Call transcripts, AI summaries, and prompts answer five key questions.
body_markdown:
You don’t need a new call analytics tool or a RevOps hire to learn why deals are won or lost. Most small teams are already sitting on the answer: every sales call is a record of what prospects care about, why deals stall, and what you’re up against. The problem isn’t missing data. It’s that no one has time to listen to it all.


With call transcripts, AI summaries, and a few good prompts on Claude, a founder or sales lead can finally ask those questions of conversations they already have.


Below, we walk through the five questions, each with a sample prompt you can run on your own calls and what to do with the answer. We also include a 30-minute weekly review routine so you can start right away.


##


5 Questions your calls can already answer with prompts


These prompts work on any recorded, transcribed call. If you’re not recording yet, the setup steps are right after the five questions. Use the insights you get for[constructive call coaching](https://www.quo.com/blog/discovery-call/) , too.


### 1. Why don’t deals close?


Most teams have a theory about why deals stall, and it’s usually drawn from one person’s memory of the last few calls. But your transcripts hold the actual reasons in the prospects’ own words.


When we ran this on our own calls that didn’t close, most weren’t rejections. Prospects were waiting for someone else to sign off or for a written quote.


**Try this prompt:**


Find a random sample of 20 recent calls that didn’t close, then list the top reasons prospects gave for not moving forward. For each reason, include how many calls it came up in and a short quote.


**What to do with it:** Look at the biggest bucket first and ask whether it’s a process problem you can fix or a mismatch you should accept. If the top reason was “needs to check with someone else,” ask earlier in the call who else is involved, and send a short recap with next steps they can forward. If prospects are waiting on a quote, send it the same day, while the call is fresh. If it’s a product or service gap, decide whether it’s one you’ll close or one you’ll accept. Price is worth checking, but don’t assume it’s the top reason until your own calls say so.


💡 **Related reading:**[How to raise prices without losing customers](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-raise-prices/)


### 2. What do prospects ask first?


It’s normal to assume you know what prospects care about. But the questions buyers open with are rarely the ones your pitch is built around. When we ran this on our own calls, most first questions were about how things would work day to day, not what they’d cost.


**Try this prompt:**


List the first three questions prospects asked in a random sample of 20 sales calls and group them by theme. For each theme, include how many calls it came up in and a short quote.


**What to do with it:** Look at the biggest theme first and check whether you answer it in the first few minutes of your calls. If buyers want to know how your service works or how hard it is to get started, lead with a quick explanation or send a one-page summary right after the call. If price leads, consider framing value before you quote a number, or mention cost in the first few minutes.


Whatever buyers ask first is usually what stands between them and trusting you.


### 3. Who are we up against?


You might have a short list of competitors in mind, but prospects can still name alternatives you wouldn’t otherwise consider. Call transcripts show who you’re really being compared to and what buyers say about them. When we ran this on our own calls, prospects were far more likely to leave something they already used than to compare us against a rival.


**Try this prompt:**


List the top 3–5 alternatives and competitor mentions across 20 recent calls, including things that aren’t companies. For each one, say whether the prospect uses it now or is considering it, whether they spoke about it positively or negatively, and how many calls it came up in.


**What to do with it:** Start with the alternative that comes up most and look at how prospects describe it. If prospects keep complaining about the same thing in what they use now, that’s what they’ll judge you on, so make sure you actually fix it and show them how early in the call. If they like a competitor’s price or offerings, decide whether you can match it. If you can’t, give a short, honest reason for why, and accept that some prospects aren’t a fit.


### 4. What did we promise?


Every sales call ends with commitments. You might promise a callback, a quote, or a timeline. When we ran this on our own calls, most of what our team promised was something to send after the call. That’s also what a lot of stalled deals were waiting on.


**Try this prompt:**


List the commitments our team made across 20 recent calls, grouped by type. For each one, include who made it, the date, and a short quote.


**What to do with it:** Compare the list against what actually happened. For each commitment, check whether you delivered it and whether it was accurate. Follow-ups that slipped are a process fix, like logging[Tasks](https://www.quo.com/blog/quo-task-examples/) right after the call or sending a recap while it’s fresh. Claims you weren’t sure about are worth verifying and then adding to a shared set of approved answers so every rep says the same thing.


**One caution:** AI can read a casual comment as a firm promise, so check anything important against the transcript.


### 5. What catches them off guard on price?


“Too expensive” lumps together objections that need different fixes. A prospect might balk at an hourly rate, a trip fee, a deposit, or an unexpected charge. When we ran this on our own calls, most pushback wasn’t about the total. It came when pricing worked differently than they’d assumed, like how they’d be billed.


**Try this prompt:**


Find moments across 20 recent calls where a prospect pushed back on cost or scope, and say what they were reacting to. For each one, include how many calls it came up in and a short quote.


**What to do with it:** Start with the biggest trends and look for where the prospect’s expectations and your pricing didn’t line up. If they assumed you charge one way and you charge another, like per person instead of per job, explain how your pricing works before you give a number. If the issue is paying up front, offer a monthly option, a smaller deposit, or a smaller first job.


**A caution:** As with any 20-call sample, treat the counts as a pattern, not a precise measurement. Run the prompt again next month to see whether the trends have changed.


##


How to set up your calls to run these prompts


Every prompt above runs[AI call analysis](https://www.quo.com/blog/ai-to-analyze-phone-calls/) on recorded, transcribed calls. Here’s the setup, in order:


- **Turn on**[sales call recordings](https://www.quo.com/blog/sales-call-recordings/) **.** Decide which calls to record. For most teams, that’s every inbound and outbound sales call.
- **Enable** **speech-to-text** **transcripts and summaries.** Do this before you start building your call library, since calls recorded earlier won’t have transcripts.
- **Add**[AI call tags](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/call-tagging) **for** **topic detection** **.** Tags sort calls by topic or outcome, so you can run a prompt on a specific set, like every call where pricing came up.
- **Connect Claude.** This lets you or your sales lead ask questions across all of those calls and get[Claude call insights](https://www.quo.com/blog/quo-claude-call-insights/) in plain English.


**A note on consent.** Many states require everyone on a call to agree to be recorded. This is often called two-party or all-party consent. Laws vary by state and country, so play it safe by letting callers know they’re being recorded at the start of each call.


##


Building the habit


The insights in your calls only help if someone generates them regularly. Here’s a weekly routine that takes about 30 minutes:


1. **Run one or two prompts.** You don’t need to run all five questions every week. Rotate them, or run the one that matches your biggest question right now. Skim a few transcripts to check the AI’s answers.
2. **Decide on one change.** Pick a single action from what you found. This could be a new line in your opener, a faster follow-up, or a clearer way to explain pricing. One change you actually make beats a long list you don’t.
3. **Keep a record.** Maintain a log of changes and key findings where your team can see it.


##


When you need a revenue intelligence platform


This routine has limits, and we want to be straightforward about that. If your team has grown, you may want to consider switching to a revenue intelligence platform for more consistent tracking. If you need more advanced tools for pipeline inspection, forecasting, or sentiment analysis, you may need to invest in a platform like[Gong](https://www.quo.com/integrations/gong) .


What Quo gives you is call logging, recordings, transcripts, and summaries. You also get AI call tags — on the Scale plan — and the Claude connector. That means you build the analysis workflow yourself using our questions and weekly review as a springboard to get started.

##


FAQs


**Do small teams need conversation intelligence software?**


Usually not at the start. A team of two to 15 reps can get insights from call transcripts and summaries, plus the right prompts on Claude. Conversation intelligence software isn’t worth it if you have a small team and don’t need pipeline inspection or forecasting.


**How do I analyze sales calls with AI?**


Record your calls and get transcripts and summaries. Then ask an AI assistant a specific question across a set of calls, such as “What objections came up in the last 20 calls?” It’s better to ask specific questions rather than make open requests to summarize everything. The AI will pull out patterns you can act on instead of recapping what you already know.
